query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, aluminum‐resistant protective interlayer to boride-based components via chemical vapor deposition (CVD) will reduce molten-aluminum corrosion during hot-dip aluminum plating.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional boride-based components without any engineered surface interlayer, which are vulnerable to direct attack by molten aluminum at plating temperatures (~660°C).
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, uniform aluminum-resistant coating (e.g., a nitride or oxide layer that is stable at high temperatures) via chemical vapor deposition onto the surface of boride components.
generation.conditions: Exposure in hot-dip aluminum-plating environments with prolonged contact of molten aluminum at approximately 660°C under typical industrial processing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, well-adhered interlayer that acts as a diffusion and chemical reaction barrier between the boride substrate and the molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The protective interlayer limits direct contact between the boride surface and molten aluminum, thereby reducing deleterious interfacial reactions, metal diffusion, and subsequent corrosion processes. This barrier effect stabilizes the surface and prevents the formation of corrosion pits and intermetallic phases that would degrade the component.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated boride components should show a measurable improvement in corrosion resistance – such as a lower corrosion current density, reduced weight loss, and fewer surface defects during/after exposure to molten aluminum – relative to uncoated components.
generation.baseline: Boride components produced by conventional processing, without any additional protective surface layer, tested under similar molten aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected as long as the coating remains uniform, well-adhered, and intact under continuous exposure at ~660°C. The intervention may be less effective if the coating degrades due to thermal stresses or if its thickness is not optimized.
generation.uncertainty: The ideal coating material, thickness, and processing parameters need further optimization. There is also some uncertainty regarding long-term adhesion and potential delamination under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based components: one set with the CVD-deposited aluminum-resistant interlayer and one set without any coating. Subject both sets to continuous immersion in molten aluminum (approximately 660°C) under conditions that mimic hot-dip aluminum plating. After a predetermined exposure period, analyze surface morphology, quantify weight loss, measure corrosion current density, and perform microstructural analysis (e.g., via SEM) to assess the extent of corrosion and interfacial degradation.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion parameters (e.g., corrosion current density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated components do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher weight loss, corrosion current density, and surface degradation) compared to the uncoated baseline under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, a reinforced layer on the surface of HEA was successfully synthesized by powder-pack boriding. The microstructure, microhardness, wear resistance, and boriding mechanism were investigated. The following conclusions can be summarized: The microstructure of the surface layer is mainly composed of MB-type boride and M2B-type boride. The original interface of the surface layer is located at the interface between the BL and the diffusion layer, where element B diffuses inward and metal elements diffuse outward. The activation energy and frequency factor of the B element in CoCrFeMnNi HEA are 206.93 kJ/mol and 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s, respectively. Increasing the boronizing duration and temperature resulted in an increase in the BL and diffusion layer thickness. The surface strengthening of CoCrFeMnNi HEA was achieved by the boriding treatment. Its surface microhardness has significantly increased from 3.9 ± 0.1 Gpa to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa. The surface layer shows a lower friction coefficient of 0.48 than that of the substrate (0.86). Depending on the wear mechanism, adhesive wear mainly occurs in unboronized samples, and abrasive wear is the main wear mechanism in boronized samples. Th

In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

chosen.lever: surface modification via a protective interlayer
chosen.technique: chemical vapor deposition (CVD) to apply an aluminum-resistant coating
chosen.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical plating temperatures (~660°C) during prolonged immersion tests replicating hot-dip plating conditions
chosen.why: This move directly fills the niche of identifying a single, practical intervention to improve molten-aluminum corrosion resistance by addressing the interface between the boride substrate and molten aluminum. The use of CVD to deposit a protective, Al-resistant interlayer is a standard and scalable method in materials science. It reverses the gap in previous studies that may have only characterized bulk boride behavior by focusing on surface interfacial modifications under realistic operating conditions, and it provides a controlled experiment that can falsify the proposed mechanism by comparing coated versus uncoated components.
